[PATH:empirical] World Bank's AidData: 'Buying Influence? The Political Economy of Tied Aid' (empirical panel study of aid effectiveness in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia since 2000, with focus on procurement conditions) — Directly tests the causal link between tied aid and poverty reduction outcomes in stable democracies, controlling for governance quality and procurement rules.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review: 'The Impact of Tied vs. Untied Aid on Poverty Alleviation in Democratic Recipient Countries' (meta-analysis of 20+ econometric studies, focusing on Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia since 2000) — Aggregates existing empirical evidence to determine whether the relationship is robust across different contexts and methodologies, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model: 'Procurement Constraints and Local Welfare: A General Equilibrium Approach' (simulates effects of donor procurement rules on market inefficiencies and income distribution in stable democracies) — Provides causal mechanisms explaining why tied aid might fail to reduce extreme poverty, offering testable predictions and filling gaps where empirical data is scarce.

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Development Research Group: Aid Effectiveness and Poverty Reduction Datasets — Provides cross-country panel data on official development assistance and poverty indices in stable democracies post-1990, enabling regression analysis to test causal links between aid flows and extreme poverty reduction.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of aid effectiveness in democratic contexts (e.g., Journal of Development Economics, 2015-2024) — Synthesizes existing studies that isolate the moderating effect of political stability and democratic institutions on aid-poverty relationships, highlighting methodological disagreements that underpin the disputed status.

[PATH:empirical] Case-control comparison of aid programs in stable democracies vs. fragile states (e.g., USAID evaluations matched via propensity scores) — Tests the hypothesis directly by comparing poverty outcomes in stable democracies with similar countries receiving equivalent aid, controlling for governance quality and time trends since the Cold War.

C007.subject: Foreign aid provided as direct budget support
C007.predicate: reduces domestic tax revenue collection and weakens institutional accountability
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Foreign aid provided as direct budget support fiscal self-sufficiency in recipient countries]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel data analysis of tax-to-GDP ratios before and after the introduction of budget support in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia (e.g., using IMF Government Finance Statistics and World Bank data) — This would directly test whether periods of high budget-support aid correlate with declines in domestic tax revenue, controlling for other factors like economic shocks or governance reforms.

[PATH:theoretical] Case studies or process-tracing of donor conditionalities attached to budget support in selected countries (e.g., Ghana, Tanzania, Uganda) examining effects on parliamentary oversight and public financial management reforms — Theoretical work on fiscal sovereignty and accountability suggests budget support may bypass domestic revenue-raising incentives and weaken institutions; these cases would allow testing the causal mechanisms linking aid modality to accountability outcomes.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of existing literature on the 'resource curse' and foreign aid, focusing on studies that compare budget support with project aid in terms of fiscal self-sufficiency and institutional quality — A meta-analysis of published and grey literature would synthesize available evidence, identify gaps, and assess whether the disputed relationship holds across different contexts and methodologies.

C008.subject: Foreign aid
C008.predicate: can break cycles of poverty and catalyze self-sustaining growth
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Foreign aid long-term poverty reduction]

[PATH:empirical] Systematic review of randomized controlled trials on cash transfers and infrastructure aid in sub-Saharan Africa (e.g., via 3ie Impact Evaluation Repository) — Provides causal evidence on whether unconditional or conditional aid directly reduces poverty metrics over 10-15 years, testing the 'break cycles' claim.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel data analysis using AidData and World Bank indicators (e.g., Burnside & Dollar replication studies) — Allows econometric testing of long-term associations between aid flows and poverty reduction in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, controlling for governance and external shocks.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of poverty traps and aid effectiveness (e.g., Sachs vs. Easterly debates; Journal of Development Economics) — Evaluates mechanisms (e.g., investment vs. dependency) that underpin the hypothesis, clarifying conditions under which aid catalyzes self-sustaining growth.
